q: A singleton service takes a scoped `DbContext` in its constructor. What goes wrong, and what is the right design?

The singleton captures one DbContext for the whole application lifetime, so it is shared across concurrent requests (DbContext is scoped and not thread-safe), which causes errors and corrupted state. Make the service scoped (or create a scope per operation, or use IDbContextFactory).
Why return `TypedResults.NotFound()` for another user's note instead of `Forbidden`, and where must the ownership check live?

A 404 does not confirm that the record exists, which limits information leakage. The ownership check must be in the data access or handler for every request (for example filtering the query by the current user id), because authorisation policies alone only say the user may call the endpoint.
Why does the same middleware order matter in ASP.NET Core as in Express, and what is one concrete wrong order?

The pipeline runs middleware in registration order, so a layer registered too late is never reached by earlier responses. For example, `UseAuthorization` before `UseAuthentication` finds no authenticated user, and CORS placed after an endpoint answers without CORS headers.

## Why it exists

**C#** is a statically typed, garbage-collected, general-purpose language, and **.NET** is the platform it runs on: the runtime, the standard libraries and the command-line tools. It is one of the most widely used languages for **business backends** (ASP.NET Core web APIs), **cloud and Azure services**, **desktop and mobile apps** (WPF, WinForms, .NET MAUI), **game development** (the Unity engine uses C# for scripting) and large internal enterprise systems. Modern .NET is **open source and cross-platform**: the same code builds and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, in containers, and on ARM and x64.

If you know Python or TypeScript, C# will feel familiar and a little more formal. The big differences: types are checked **before** the program runs, code is compiled to an intermediate form that the runtime just-in-time compiles, and a project has an explicit file that says what to build. In return you get strong tooling (refactoring, analysers, a superb debugger), high performance, and a very consistent standard library.

**Important:** unlike the other lessons in this batch, **no .NET SDK exists in the sandbox where this lesson was written**, so none of the C# code below was compiled or run. The code was written conservatively using long-stable syntax and checked against Microsoft's documentation where it uses newer features; the single output shown was traced by hand and is labelled that way. Treat it as carefully reviewed but not executed, and run it yourself (`dotnet run`) as the first exercise.

**Mental model:** C# is a **well-organised workshop**. The **SDK** is the toolbox (compiler, build system, package manager). The **runtime** is the machine that actually runs your compiled program and cleans up memory for you. **NuGet** is the supply cabinet for third-party parts. A **project file** (`.csproj`) is the work order.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

### The toolchain and the project file

You install the **.NET SDK** (it includes the runtime). As of the date of this lesson, **.NET 10 is the current Long-Term Support release**: released on 11 November 2025 and supported until 14 November 2028, according to Microsoft's .NET support policy page. .NET 9 and .NET 8 both reach end of support on 10 November 2026, so new projects should target `net10.0`. Even-numbered releases are LTS, odd-numbered ones are shorter-lived, and a new major version arrives each November, so check the support policy page when you start a project.

Everything is driven by the `dotnet` command:

- `dotnet new console -o OrdersReport` creates a project from a template, `dotnet run` builds and runs it, `dotnet build` only compiles, `dotnet watch` rebuilds on save.
- `dotnet add package <name>` installs a library from **NuGet**, `dotnet test` runs the tests, `dotnet publish -c Release` produces the files to deploy.
- `dotnet --list-sdks` and `dotnet --info` show what is installed, which is the first thing to check when "it works on my machine".

The project file is XML and short for a modern project:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

`TargetFramework` says which .NET version the code targets. `Nullable` turns on **nullable reference types** (below). `ImplicitUsings` adds the common `using` statements automatically. A **solution** (`.sln`) groups several projects (for instance the API, a library and the tests). Newer SDKs can also run a single `.cs` file directly, as a "file-based app", which is handy for scripts; check the .NET 10 documentation for the details.

### The language in one sweep

- **Types.** Every variable has a type, known at compile time. `var` lets the compiler infer it (`var count = 3;` is still an `int`). **Value types** (`int`, `decimal`, `bool`, structs, enums) are copied on assignment; **reference types** (classes, strings, arrays, records) share one object.
- **Numbers for money.** Use `decimal` for currency (exact base-10 arithmetic, the `m` suffix as in `1.50m`), never `double`, for the same floating-point reasons as in the formats lesson.
- **Nullable reference types.** With `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`, a plain `string` means "never null" and `string?` means "may be null". The compiler warns when you might dereference null, which removes most `NullReferenceException` crashes at build time. Treat these warnings as errors in serious projects.
- **Records.** `record Order(int Id, string Customer, ...)` declares an immutable data type with value-based equality, a readable `ToString()`, and a `with` expression to make modified copies. Records are the default choice for data transfer objects and domain values.
- **Collections and LINQ.** `List<T>`, `Dictionary<K,V>`, `HashSet<T>`; and **LINQ** (language-integrated query) gives you `Where`, `Select`, `GroupBy`, `OrderBy`, `Sum` and friends on any sequence, much like array methods in JavaScript or comprehensions in Python. LINQ queries are **lazy**: they run when enumerated, not when written.
- **Pattern matching.** `switch` expressions with relational patterns (`>= 30m => "large"`), type patterns, property patterns and `is not null` checks replace long `if` chains.
- **Exceptions and `using`.** `try/catch/finally` as usual; types that hold resources (files, connections) implement `IDisposable` and are released with `using var file = ...;`.
- **async/await.** Exactly the idea from the JavaScript async lesson: a method returning `Task<T>` can `await` other tasks without blocking a thread. `Task.WhenAll(...)` is `Promise.all`.
- **Generics, interfaces and dependency injection.** You program against interfaces (`INoteStore`) and let a container supply implementations; ASP.NET Core has this built in (next lesson).

### Where it differs from Python and JavaScript

| Idea | Python / JavaScript | C# |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typing | dynamic (types optional in TS) | static, checked at compile time |
| Null | `None` / `null`, `undefined` | `null`, with nullable reference types as a compile-time check |
| Data class | `dataclass` / object literal | `record` |
| Collections pipeline | list comprehension / `.map().filter()` | LINQ (`Select`, `Where`) |
| Concurrency | `asyncio` / Promises | `Task` and `async`/`await`, plus real threads |
| Packages | pip / npm | NuGet |
| Run | interpreter | compile to IL, then JIT-compile at run time (ahead-of-time options exist) |
| Project file | `pyproject.toml` / `package.json` | `.csproj` |

### What is new in C# 14

C# 14 ships with .NET 10 (you need the .NET 10 SDK to use it). According to Microsoft's "What's new in C# 14" page, among other additions it brings the `field` keyword (a property accessor can refer to its own compiler-generated backing field without declaring one), **extension members** (extension properties and static members, not just methods) and **null-conditional assignment** (`customer?.Order = LoadOrder();` assigns only if `customer` is not null). Short illustrations, following the documented syntax:

```csharp
// C# 14 / .NET 10 SDK required. Not compiled in this lesson's sandbox.
public class Person
{
    // 'field' is the hidden backing field: no manual private string _name needed.
    public string Name
    {
        get;
        set => field = value?.Trim() ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(value));
    }
}

public static class StringExtensions
{
    extension(string text)             // an extension block: members that look like part of string
    {
        public bool IsBlank => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text);
    }
}
```

Learn the older features well first. These are conveniences, and most production code today is written without them.

## Worked example

Goal: a small console program that groups orders by customer, ranks them by revenue and classifies each order's size, using records, LINQ and a switch expression. Create it with `dotnet new console -o OrdersReport`, replace `Program.cs` with this code and run `dotnet run`. Top-level statements come first and type declarations last, as the language requires.

```csharp
var orders = new List<Order>
{
    new(1, "Ada",   "Pen",  3,  1.50m),
    new(2, "Linus", "Book", 1, 12.00m),
    new(3, "Ada",   "Lamp", 1, 30.00m),
    new(4, "Grace", "Pen", 10,  1.40m),
};

var revenueByCustomer = orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.Customer)
    .Select(g => new { Customer = g.Key, Revenue = g.Sum(o => o.Total) })
    .OrderByDescending(x => x.Revenue);

foreach (var row in revenueByCustomer)
    Console.WriteLine($"{row.Customer,-6} {row.Revenue,8:F2}");

foreach (var o in orders)
    Console.WriteLine($"#{o.Id}: {Size(o)}");

static string Size(Order o) => o.Total switch
{
    >= 30m => "large",
    >= 10m => "medium",
    _      => "small",
};

record Order(int Id, string Customer, string Product, int Qty, decimal UnitPrice)
{
    public decimal Total => Qty * UnitPrice;
}
```

Expected output, **traced by hand and not run** (Ada's orders total 4.50 + 30.00, Grace's 14.00, Linus's 12.00):

```text
Ada       34.50
Grace     14.00
Linus     12.00
#1: small
#2: medium
#3: large
#4: medium
```

What each part shows:

- The **record** gives `Order` a constructor, immutable properties and a computed `Total` in one declaration. `new(1, "Ada", ...)` uses a target-typed `new`, because the list's element type is already known.
- **LINQ** reads as a pipeline: group, project to an anonymous type, sort descending. Nothing executes until the `foreach` enumerates it (deferred execution).
- `{row.Customer,-6}` pads the name to 6 characters, left-aligned, and `{row.Revenue,8:F2}` right-aligns the revenue in 8 characters with two decimals: interpolated strings carry their formatting inside the braces.
- The **switch expression** with relational patterns covers every case (`_` is the default), and the compiler warns if a case is missing.

A unit test with **xUnit** (create it with `dotnet new xunit`, reference the main project, run `dotnet test`):

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class OrderTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Total_multiplies_quantity_by_unit_price()
    {
        var order = new Order(1, "Ada", "Pen", 3, 1.50m);
        Assert.Equal(4.50m, order.Total);
    }
}
```

An async variant, mirroring `Promise.all` from the JavaScript lesson (also unrun):

```csharp
static async Task<decimal> GetPriceAsync(string sku)
{
    await Task.Delay(100);                       // stands in for a network call
    return sku == "pen" ? 1.50m : 12.00m;
}

var skus = new[] { "pen", "book", "pen" };
decimal[] prices = await Task.WhenAll(skus.Select(GetPriceAsync));   // all three run concurrently
Console.WriteLine(prices.Sum());
```

## In real products

- **Web APIs and services** with ASP.NET Core (the next lesson) are the most common use: banks, insurers, logistics, SaaS products and internal tools, often hosted on Azure but equally on AWS, on-premises or in containers.
- **Desktop and mobile apps:** WPF and WinForms for Windows desktop software, .NET MAUI for cross-platform mobile and desktop, Blazor for web UI written in C#.
- **Games:** Unity scripts are C#, which makes C# one of the most common first languages in game development.
- **Cloud and automation:** Azure Functions, background workers, command-line tools, data pipelines, and infrastructure SDKs.
- **Performance-sensitive code:** the runtime's JIT compiler, spans and value types make C# fast, and ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation can reduce start-up time and memory for containers and serverless functions at the cost of some reflection-based features.
- **Team practices:** analysers and `dotnet format` enforce style in CI, NuGet packages are versioned and sometimes hosted in a private feed, and long-lived systems follow the LTS schedule: upgrade before end of support.

> [!pitfall] Blocking on async code (`.Result`, `.Wait()`, `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`) and `async void`. Blocking threads can cause deadlocks in some app types and thread starvation under load in servers, and an exception thrown from an `async void` method cannot be caught by the caller. Use `async Task` all the way up and `await` every task.

> [!pitfall] Using `double` for money, `DateTime` for instants across time zones, or culture-sensitive string comparison. Use `decimal`, `DateTimeOffset` (or UTC), and `StringComparison.Ordinal` or `OrdinalIgnoreCase` when comparing identifiers, so the program behaves the same on every server and in every locale.

> [!pitfall] Enumerating a LINQ query many times, or building it from a database and forgetting it is lazy. A deferred query re-runs its source each time, can see changed data, and may issue repeated database calls. Call `.ToList()` when you want a snapshot, and measure before assuming a query is cheap.

> [!pitfall] Creating a new `HttpClient` for every request (it exhausts sockets) or never disposing `IDisposable` objects. Reuse a single `HttpClient` or use `IHttpClientFactory`, and wrap disposable resources in `using`.

> [!tip] Turn on `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` and treat warnings as errors from the first day (`<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>`), keep records immutable, prefer small methods with clear names, and let the IDE (Visual Studio, VS Code with the C# extension, or JetBrains Rider) refactor and analyse. Read compiler errors top to bottom; the first one usually causes the rest.

> [!tip] Learn by running the official tutorials in a scratch project: `dotnet new console`, change something, `dotnet run`, repeat. Use `dotnet watch` for fast feedback, `dotnet test` from the start, and the debugger instead of print statements for anything non-trivial.

> [!cost] .NET itself is free and open source, but costs appear elsewhere: hosting (a .NET app in a container is cheap, but memory settings matter), commercial IDE or tooling licences if you choose them, and the effort of keeping up with the yearly release cadence. Staying on an unsupported version (such as .NET 8 or 9 after 10 November 2026) is a hidden cost, since security fixes stop. Check licensing terms of any third-party NuGet package, because some popular libraries have moved to commercial licences.

> [!security] Packages come from NuGet, so apply the supply-chain habits from the security lessons: pin versions, use lock files, review new dependencies, prefer well-maintained packages, and scan with `dotnet list package --vulnerable`. Never deserialize untrusted data with unsafe serializers (the old `BinaryFormatter` is obsolete and dangerous), use parameterised queries or an ORM for SQL, keep secrets out of source control (user-secrets in development, a vault such as Azure Key Vault in production), and keep the runtime patched.

> [!prod] Production checklist: target the current LTS and plan upgrades before end of support; nullable reference types and analysers enabled with warnings as errors; central package management and a lock file; unit tests in CI (`dotnet test`) with coverage; structured logging; configuration and secrets from the environment, not code; `dotnet publish -c Release` in a reproducible container build; health checks; and a documented procedure for patching the runtime image.

> [!version] Researched 2026-10-23 from Microsoft's official pages as returned by web search: the .NET support policy (.NET 10 is LTS, released 11 November 2025, supported until 14 November 2028; .NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on 10 November 2026) and the "What's new in C# 14" page (the `field` keyword, extension members, null-conditional assignment). The even/odd LTS pattern and the yearly November cadence are consistent with those pages but stated from general knowledge. NOT verified: exact C# 14 syntax beyond the documented forms, file-based app details, AOT trade-offs, `dotnet list package --vulnerable` output, third-party package licence changes, and the linked resources, which could not be opened from the sandbox. Run the examples yourself before relying on them.
q: Why should money be stored in `decimal` rather than `double` in C#?

double is binary floating point and cannot represent many base-10 fractions exactly (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3). decimal does exact base-10 arithmetic (written with an m suffix such as 1.50m), which is what currency calculations need.
What does enabling nullable reference types change, and what does `string?` mean?

The compiler tracks whether references may be null: a plain `string` is expected to never be null, `string?` may be null, and you get warnings where you might dereference a possible null. Most NullReferenceExceptions become build-time warnings.
A web endpoint calls an async method with `.Result` inside a controller. What can go wrong and what is the fix?
Blocking a thread while waiting for the task can deadlock in some contexts and starves the thread pool under load. Make the method `async Task<T>` and `await` the call all the way up the stack.

dg.cap: A spectrum of trade-offs between productivity and control. Most business services are I/O-bound, so team skills and ecosystem usually decide.
n: Balanced: Go, Java, C#, Kotlin (static types, GC)
Control and safety: Rust (ownership, no GC)
Maximum control: C and C++ (manual memory)

q: What does Rust's ownership system guarantee, and what does it cost?

At compile time it ensures memory is freed exactly once, with no use-after-free or data races in safe code, and no garbage collector. The cost is a steeper learning curve, longer compile times and a smaller talent pool.
How do Go goroutines differ from OS threads?
Goroutines are very cheap functions multiplexed by the Go runtime onto a few OS threads, so thousands or millions can run. Channels and the context package handle communication and cancellation.
What do Java virtual threads change?
Since Java 21 they let simple blocking code scale like async code, because each task gets a lightweight thread that the JVM schedules onto a few carrier threads.
Why are errors handled differently in Go and Rust compared with Java or Python?
Go and Rust return errors as values (error, Result) and make you handle them explicitly, so control flow is visible. Java, C# and Python use exceptions that unwind the stack implicitly.
When does language speed matter least?
For I/O-bound services dominated by database queries, network calls and architecture. Measure the real bottleneck before switching languages.
What are the main criteria for choosing a language for a new service?
Team skills and operability, the ecosystem for the problem, measured performance needs, unacceptable failure modes such as memory unsafety, and long-term maintenance and deployment.
